{
  "need": "Identity",
  "secondary": { "name": "Belonging", "description": "They want to know if you are a safe person to be real with — someone who will still be in their corner even when the conversation gets uncomfortable." },
  "read": "Your kid is trying to figure out who they are and who they are allowed to become, and they came to you — the person who matters most — to do that work out loud. When you froze, the message they likely received was that the question was too dangerous to touch, or that you see yourself as above the conversation. That lands as a status wound: they risked being honest with you and got a wall back.",
  "pull": { "collapse": "Protector", "instinct": "Dodge it, change the subject, or give a vague non-answer to keep the peace — which protects your own comfort but teaches them that honesty with you has a ceiling." },
  "mentorMove": "Go back to them and open the door yourself, on your terms. You do not have to share every detail, but you do have to be real enough that they know you are a person who has actually lived, not a parent playing a role.",
  "holdFirm": [
    "You will not pretend the freeze did not happen — you owe them a real return to the conversation.",
    "You will not rewrite your past into a tidy lesson that conveniently lines up with whatever you want them to do right now."
  ],
  "stayFlexible": [
    "You get to decide how much detail is appropriate for their age and your relationship — sharing the emotional truth does not require a full confession.",
    "You can reopen the conversation whenever and wherever feels right: at dinner, in the car, on a walk — pick the setting where they are most likely to actually hear you."
  ],
  "forceLevel": { "level": 1, "label": "Empathy" },
  "script": [
    { "phase": "Connection", "words": "Hey, I've been thinking about what you asked me the other day and the fact that I just kind of shut down. That wasn't fair to you and I want to try again." },
    { "phase": "Curiosity", "words": "Can I ask what made you want to bring that up? I'm not looking for a certain answer — I genuinely want to know what was going on in your head." },
    { "phase": "Collaboration", "words": "Here's what's true from my end: yes, I did some things at your age that I'm not proud of, and some that I'm still sorting out. I froze because I didn't want to say the wrong thing, not because I was hiding from you. That's on me, not on the question." },
    { "phase": "Commitment", "words": "I want us to be able to talk about the hard stuff — the real stuff — and that means I have to be willing to go first sometimes. I'm holding both of us to that standard because I think you can handle honesty and I think I can too. If something comes up again and you want to dig into it, come find me. I'll stay in it with you." }
  ],
  "longGame": "Every time you walk back into an uncomfortable conversation instead of away from it, you are showing them that difficult questions do not have to be carried alone — and that is the exact model you want them to have when the stakes are much higher than your history."
}
situation: My teenager asked me a hard question about something I did at their age, and I froze instead of answering.
